newsitem.title: USA: Key U.S. senator sees consensus emerging on tobacco.
newsitem.headline: Key U.S. senator sees consensus emerging on tobacco.

text.p: An influential U.S. senator said Wednesday there was a consensus growing in Congress to use the proposed tobacco settlement to combat youth smoking instead of relying on lawsuits with unpredictable results.

"The lines of consensus are starting to emerge," said Orrin Hatch, the Utah Republican who is chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee. "Can we afford to fritter away the opportunity to stop 3,000 kids a day from (starting) smoking?"

In a Judiciary Committee hearing and in comments to reporters, Hatch said he and other lawmakers would seek changes in the far-reaching pact negotiated in June by the tobacco industry and the 40 state attorneys general suing it.

The only specific change he mentioned was stronger language guaranteeing the Food and Drug Administration power to regulate nicotine, a change also demanded by the White House, lawmakers and public health advocates.
"If we do nothing, what is the acceptable alternative?" Hatch said, noting that relying on lawsuits was uncertain.

His comments came a day after former U.S. Surgeon General C. Everett Koop and former FDA chief David Kessler urged lawmakers to start over and craft a national tobacco policy instead of tinkering with what they called a "flawed" settlement.

Although the proposal will continue to shift as congressional hearings continue this fall, a variety of congressional and health sources said it seems likely that any legislation would also include steeper penalties if the industry fails to meet targets for cutting youth smoking.

There may also be some tougher provisions for disclosure of confidential industry documents and possibly some modifications of the tax deductibility of the industry payments, public health and congressional sources said.

An economist who testified, Jeffrey Harris of the Massachusetts Institutes of Technology, said the settlement calling for cigarette makers to pay $368.5 billion to settle state lawsuits would actually cost the industry about $194.5 billion -- less if tax deductions are taken into account.
He said it would lead to about a 62-cent-a-pack price increase, which would probably not be enough to meet the goals for reducing teen smoking.

The Judiciary Committee heard a broad range of views on the pact, from the American Medical Association to convenience store owners. According to Dr. Lonnie Bristow, a past president of the AMA and a participant in the settlement talks, the AMA on Thursday will "support the basic structure" of the settlement proposal but recommend some changes.

Representing the convenience stores, which sell more than half of the packs of cigarettes and tobacco sold in the United States each year, Virginia store owner Duncan Thomas complained the retailers had not been part of the settlement talks, and that the deal would make a legal product "effectively invisible within our industry's retail outlets."

Also Wednesday, Democratic Sens. Wendell Ford of Kentucky and Charles Robb of Virginia, along with other members of Congress from tobacco-growing states, wrote to President Clinton to stick to anti-youth smoking goals and not to restrict "adult choice."

Some critics of the settlement proposal fear it could lead to an outright ban on nicotine. Others have criticized it as not tough enough. The settlement needs approval from the White House and Congress, where laws are needed to enact it.

Meanwhile, the Institute of Policy Studies released a study saying tobacco executives would "stand to profit tremendously" from the probable rise in tobacco stock prices if the settlement is enacted, while taxpayers would foot much of the bill.

"The executives want the public and Congress to believe that for them the proposed deal is a' bitter pill,'" said Sarah Anderson, a co-author of the report from the liberal think tank. "In reality, it will be a huge windfall."
